newsitem.title: UK: Euro refiners shy to pull plug on over-capacity.
newsitem.headline: Euro refiners shy to pull plug on over-capacity.

text.p: The European oil refining industry is still hampered by substantial surplus capacity but no operator is rushing to close down plants, consultants Enerfinance said on Thursday.
"Choosing to close a refinery is a more difficult decision than it was 15 years ago," Enerfinance said, adding that a web of factors held operators back from pulling the plug.
Refiners say up to 60 million tonnes, or ten percent of European capacity should be closed, Paris-based Enerfinance said in its report "Oil Markets and Networks in Europe."
While refining margins may be low, they are not low enough to force closures because of many competitive risks involved, Enerfinance said.
So far this year, refining margins have averaged around $1.80 per barrel for a typical European refinery. Enerfinance reckons 1997 margins will range between $1.60-$1.80.
At this level, refinery closures will be few and far between and necessary widespread restructuring will not occur, the report said.
"Although it is probable that one or two closures will be announced in 1997, the impact will not reach the 30 million tonnes that Enerfinance has judged necessary for improvement in margins."

Companies such as Texaco, Fina, Total and the newly merged British Petroleum /Mobil European downstream operation have already reduced the number of their refineries to a level where new cuts may endanger their competitive position, the report said.
Another factor clouding the picture is that the most threatened refineries are not necessarily the most technologically outdated.
A healthy hydroskimming margin over the last year has squeezed the profitability differential between Europe's least and most sophisticated refineries, Enerfinanace said.
As a consequence, some of the less sophisticated units are able to make a better return on capital than some of the more sophisticated sites which have invested heavily in conversion.
A decision to close a particular refinery would be a gift to other operators in the region, Enerfinance said.

"The refiner that closes his site would support the cost of such a decision alone, and would undoubtedly contribute to a restoration of the level of margins, from which he, no longer in the region, would not secure a profit," the report said.
"An oil company has to ensure that any advantage gained from a closure is not less than one gained by a competitor."
